extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly; educated general public; students and scholars of anthropology, art history, and aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and indicators for judging stages of aesthetic development in humans and societies, from nascent mate-focused tastes through ornamentation of person and implements to architecture, religion-backed arts, and appreciation of landscape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of aesthetic taste via sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste for bright hues, musical sound, or other ornaments may originate in sexual selection — preferences developed in choosing mates (e.g., preference for brighter coloration or sweeter/louder song).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: birds preferring sweetest/loudest singers; transferred taste for bright hues from foraging to mate choice; ornamental traits (plumage, antlers, song) develop by small gradations so long as they do not impair organism efficiency. The strongest and best tend to be most beautiful, reinforcing sexual and natural selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of beauty centered on mates (primitive anthropocentrism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Primitive aesthetic feeling is primarily anthroponmistic — gathered mainly around the person of man or woman; the human face and figure remain the central standard of beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early human appreciation strongest and most discriminative regarding mates (eyes, hair, teeth, lips, complexion). The text frames this as the 'primitive starting-point' from which aesthetic expansion occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal decoration as evidence of nascent aesthetic feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of personal ornaments (perforated shells, teeth, pebbles, worked bone, feathers, flowers) is taken as the earliest evidences of derivative aesthetic feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such objects being sought as ornaments proves they were admired; decoration makes vague admiration vivid and purposive. Modern analogies: children and savages begin to admire flowers when woven into wreaths or put in hair. Archaeological examples: palaeolithic necklaces and carved bone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body-painting, dyes, cosmetics, and mutilative ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices like ochre/woad dyeing, henna, indigo, tattooing, lip plugs, and other body modifications function as aesthetic expressions and indicators of taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These may originate in non-aesthetic (subordinative) intentions but become prized aesthetically (women valuing tattooing or lip ornaments). Quoted anecdotes (New Zealand girls) illustrate aesthetic motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornamentation of weapons and personal implements
rubrics_metrics.description: Delight in beauty transferred to weapons and personal utensils: intentional selection of materials (colored jaspers, greenstone, agate, obsidian), carved and polished handles, and decorative bindings indicate a higher aesthetic stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with very rude tools, substantial extra labor expended for ornamentation signals aesthetic care (palaeolithic hatchets, Australian boomerangs, Admiralty Island staves). Considered 'second human stage' of aesthetic development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decoration of domestic vessels and pottery
rubrics_metrics.description: Decoration of calabashes, cocoanuts, and pottery — often molded with lines or string-courses from the outset — marks a further step beyond personal implements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are 'one degree less personal' than weapons and indicate slightly higher stage; examples include graceful Central African specimens and prehistoric pottery considered models for later ware.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decoration of dwellings and interior ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: As humans dwell in huts and houses, these take on aesthetic character: ground-plans, neat finishes (e.g., Esquimau snow-houses), and internal display (drawing/dining rooms) show developed taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homes become ornamented when used for display; state-apartments and palaces concentrate best objects. The progression from personal to domestic ornamentation is a standard stage indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association of aesthetic products with royalty and divinity
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic products are early attributes of royalty and religion; palaces and temples (royal huts → palaces → monumental architecture) drive major advances in arts like architecture, sculpture, and painting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architecture is called the 'central royal art'; early impressive buildings are palaces or shrines. Examples: Egyptian pyramids, Assyrian brick works, Indian palaces and mosques, Solomon's temple catalog.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional patronage and specialization of the arts
rubrics_metrics.description: When courts and temples patronize artists, arts become specialized and reach higher technical and aesthetic levels (sculpture as handmaid of architecture; painting, music linked to ecclesiastical forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Renaissance masters producing for popes and kings; royal factories (Sèvres, Gobelins); ecclesiastical music from Gregorian chant. The presence of institutional support is an indicator of advanced aesthetic culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious/temple art as highest national aesthetic expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The most splendid national expressions of art are those created for gods and worship (temples, shrines, cathedrals) — these often represent the apex of a society's aesthetic development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Karnak, Benares, Parthenon, pagan and Christian temples. Only where faith declines do palaces outshine religious buildings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progression from anthropocentrism to appreciation of nature (apanthropinization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic evolution involves a concentric widening from human-centered beauty to a disinterested love of natural beauty (landscape, scenery); this 'apanthropinization' marks a later, higher stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early art focused on human/animal figures; landscape painting and descriptive/lyric verse arrive late. The shift is exemplified by the gradual emergence of landscape as a separate pictorial genre after the Renaissance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative valuation of scenery as a marker of cultivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste for scenery on a large scale is confined to relatively few races and social classes; strong appreciation of natural beauty indicates a high and disinterested aesthetic stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author cites cultural variability: Chinese and Hindoos care little for landscape despite artistic skill; some Russians and Americans show different emphases. Thus, widespread landscape taste signals advanced aesthetic development but is culturally variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender patterns and social uses of ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: In many 'savage' communities women universally display ornaments (original aesthetic intent), while men may monopolize handsome costumes as marks of distinction (derivative, secondary use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction helps interpret social meaning of ornamentation: whether ornament is primarily aesthetic or a sign of rank/trophy-taking. Spencer's 'Ceremonial Institutions' referenced for related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as a civilizing and educational lever
rubrics_metrics.description: Love of ornament and pride in dress can be used pedagogically to elevate aesthetic feeling into other domains (children, huts, gardens); early aesthetic progress often leads to wider civilizing effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author criticizes missionaries who preach down ornament; instead they should leverage it to encourage pride in dress and pass feeling on to other aspects of life and to offspring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence of aesthetic stages (summary indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic evolution proceeds through recognizably ordered stages: (1) mate-centered tastes and personal ornament → (2) ornamented implements/weapons → (3) domestic vessel/house decoration → (4) royal/religious institutional arts (architecture, sculpture, painting, music) → (5) disinterested appreciation of nature/landscape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use presence/strength of markers at each stage (archaeological finds, ornamented tools, decorated pottery, monumental architecture, landscape art/literature) to place a society or group within this staged framework.
